config.title: Lippincott Micro Ch1 - Bacteriology (JeffMD GI relevant)
config.subtitle: Bacteriology questions sourced from Lippincott's Illustrated Q&A Review of Microbiology & Immunology

questions.stem: Physicians and state epidemiologists investigate a cluster of acute diarrheal cases in children who attend a preschool in a small Midwestern town. The children presented with fever, acute episodes of bloody diarrhea, and petechial rash or purpura. Two of the children have scanty urine output and are showing signs of renal failure. Fecal leukocytes and parasites are absent in microscopic smears, and no obvious pathogens are identified using standard microbiologic media. What is the most common infectious agent consistent with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: The answer is B: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC). This organism is associated with bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), which is affecting two of the children. HUS is primarily a disease of infancy and early childhood caused by the production of a Shiga-like toxin that binds to and kills renal endothelial cells. HUS presents as a triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia and can lead to acute renal failure. Diarrhea caused by E. coli O157:H7 is a precipitating factor and the use of antimotility drugs may increase the risk. The clinical picture of HUS can suggest a GI bleed because the stool may be grossly bloody. Urine output is reduced or absent with renal failure; petechiae, purpura, and fever are common findings. Schistocytes are markers of HUS. Standard stool culturing does not reveal the organism (sorbitol–MacConkey medium is a screening that can give a preliminary identification). Antibiotics are not effective for EHEC. Shigella dysenteriae (not S. flexneri) can also cause HUS through the production of Shiga toxin.
keypoints: ⭐ EHEC (E. coli O157:H7) causes the triad of HUS: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure
⭐ Shiga-like toxin (Stx-1/Stx-2) binds renal endothelial cells — the primary pathogenic mechanism of HUS
⭐ Do NOT treat EHEC with antibiotics or antimotility drugs — both increase the risk of HUS
Schistocytes on peripheral blood smear are a hallmark of HUS; EHEC is not detected on standard media (requires sorbitol-MacConkey)

questions.stem: The preschool in the above case only serves pasteurized milk and packaged cookies to the children and epidemiologists quickly rule out a food source as the risk factor. Which of the following is the most plausible means by which the children were infected?
choices: Contagious transmission from an infected child
Drinking water of the preschool is contaminated with the microbe
Failure to wash hands after visiting a petting zoo
Fecal–oral transmission, most likely from the restroom
Visiting the elderly in an assisted-living or nursing home facility
questions.explanation: The answer is C: Failure to wash hands after visiting a petting zoo. Cattle are the reservoirs of Escherichia coli O157:H7; they show no signs of disease and shed the organism sporadically. Humans become infected when ingesting the organism in undercooked hamburger or foods contaminated with cattle fecal material. Children can also contract the organism by contaminating their hands through petting a cow. The organism is rarely isolated from chlorinated drinking water. E. coli O157:H7 can also be transmitted person-to-person in crowded settings such as day care centers; however, direct or indirect contact with cattle feces is a more likely route.
keypoints: ⭐ Cattle are the primary reservoir for E. coli O157:H7 — they shed it without symptoms
⭐ Transmission routes: undercooked beef, feces-contaminated food/water, or direct contact with farm animals
⭐ Petting zoos are a recognized epidemiologic setting for pediatric EHEC outbreaks
Chlorination of drinking water is effective against EHEC; person-to-person spread can occur but is a less common route

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presented with indigestion and heartburn occurring shortly after meals which she treated with over-the-counter antacids. Physical examination revealed mild epigastric tenderness. A radiolabeled-urea breath test is positive. What is the most probable etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: The answer is C: Helicobacter pylori. While all of the organisms listed are associated with GI symptoms, this case is descriptive of peptic ulcer disease, which is associated with H. pylori infection. The urea breath test is positive because H. pylori produces urease, which splits radiolabeled urea into CO2 (detected in exhaled breath) and ammonia. The other organisms cause diarrheal diseases, not peptic ulcer disease.
keypoints: ⭐ H. pylori is the leading cause of peptic ulcer disease; urease activity is detected by the radiolabeled-urea breath test
⭐ H. pylori urease splits urea → CO2 (exhaled) + NH3; NH3 neutralizes gastric acid, allowing colonization
⭐ H. pylori is also the most important risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma
Treatment is triple therapy: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole)

questions.stem: What cancer is the patient in the above case (H. pylori peptic ulcer disease) at risk for as a consequence of this infection?
questions.explanation: The answer is B: Gastric adenocarcinoma. H. pylori infection is a class I carcinogen designated by the WHO. Chronic infection leads to gastritis, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and ultimately gastric adenocarcinoma. The cagA virulence factor plays a particularly important role; cagA-negative strains are significantly less associated with gastric adenocarcinoma. H. pylori is also linked to gastric MALT lymphoma. Eradication therapy reduces (but does not eliminate) cancer risk.
keypoints: ⭐ H. pylori → chronic gastritis → atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → gastric adenocarcinoma (Correa cascade)
⭐ H. pylori is a WHO class I carcinogen and the most common bacterial cause of cancer worldwide
⭐ cagA-positive strains carry significantly higher risk of gastric adenocarcinoma than cagA-negative strains
H. pylori also causes gastric MALT lymphoma, which can regress with eradication therapy alone

questions.stem: What virulence factor of H. pylori may be associated with induction of gastric adenocarcinoma?
questions.explanation: The answer is A: cagA. All the items listed are virulence factors of H. pylori. Urease breaks down urea, releasing ammonia that neutralizes gastric acids. Heat shock protein B enhances urease activity. Mucinase breaks down gastric mucus, allowing the organism to penetrate and adhere to gastric epithelial cells. Vacuolating cytotoxin (VacA) damages gastric epithelial cells and promotes inflammation. cagA is translocated into host cells where it activates signal transduction molecules and induces morphological changes. cagA-negative strains of H. pylori are significantly less associated with gastric adenocarcinoma, making cagA the virulence factor most strongly linked to carcinogenesis.
keypoints: ⭐ cagA (cytotoxin-associated gene A) is injected into gastric epithelial cells via a type IV secretion system, dysregulating cell signaling
⭐ cagA-positive strains are classified as type I (more virulent) and carry substantially higher risk of gastric cancer
⭐ VacA causes epithelial vacuolation and apoptosis; urease enables gastric survival — both are key H. pylori virulence factors
H. pylori expresses multiple virulence factors; the cagA pathogenicity island is the strongest cancer risk marker

questions.stem: Hemorrhagic colitis, hemolytic uremic syndrome, and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura are clinical manifestations of which bacterial species?
questions.explanation: The answer is B: Escherichia coli O157:H7. Of the organisms listed, only E. coli O157:H7 is associated with this constellation of symptoms. This strain produces phage-encoded Shiga toxins (Stx-1 and Stx-2) that cause hemorrhagic colitis (bloody diarrhea) and can trigger hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) — a triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure — particularly in children. TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) shares features with HUS and may result from the same toxin-mediated endothelial injury.
keypoints: ⭐ E. coli O157:H7 produces Shiga toxins (Stx-1/Stx-2) → hemorrhagic colitis + HUS (especially in children <5)
⭐ HUS triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute renal failure
⭐ Do NOT treat with antibiotics (may increase Shiga toxin release) or antimotility agents
Identified on sorbitol-MacConkey agar (O157:H7 does not ferment sorbitol, appearing colorless)

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of low grade fever, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. One day prior to the onset of symptoms, six family members had eaten at an all-you-can-eat fried chicken buffet. Two other family members (his 82-year-old mother and a 14-month-old son) had similar symptoms. Examination of a fecal smear from the patient revealed abundant fecal leukocytes. Which of the following laboratory profiles is consistent with the most likely microbial cause of this man's condition?
questions.explanation: The answer is D: Nonlactose fermenting, Gram-negative bacilli. The two most common bacterial causes of foodborne illness in the United States are Campylobacter and Salmonella. Both are associated with undercooked poultry and cause invasive (inflammatory) GI disease with the induction of fecal leukocytes. Salmonella are Gram-negative rods that are unable to ferment lactose. Campylobacters are motile, curved, Gram-negative rods that are isolated under microaerophilic conditions on selective media such as Skirrow agar. Note: option E is incorrect because Campylobacter is Gram-negative, not Gram-positive.
keypoints: ⭐ Campylobacter and Salmonella are the two most common foodborne bacterial pathogens in the United States, both linked to undercooked poultry
⭐ Both cause inflammatory diarrhea (fecal leukocytes positive) — distinguishing them from non-invasive pathogens like ETEC or V. cholerae
⭐ Salmonella is a nonlactose-fermenting, Gram-negative rod; Campylobacter is a microaerophilic, curved, Gram-negative rod
Fecal leukocytes indicate mucosal invasion — key to distinguishing inflammatory (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter) from secretory (ETEC, cholera) diarrhea

questions.stem: Which of the following medications, if taken by the man in the above case (foodborne illness from fried chicken), could have increased his susceptibility to the infection he developed?
questions.explanation: The answer is B: Antacids. Decreased gastric acid increases susceptibility to GI disease caused by Salmonella and Vibrio. The elderly and young children are also at an increased risk of infection. Gastric acid is a critical first-line defense against ingested pathogens; reducing it with antacids, proton pump inhibitors, or H2 blockers lowers the infectious dose needed to cause disease.
keypoints: ⭐ Gastric acid is a key innate host defense against enteric pathogens — its reduction (antacids, PPIs, H2 blockers) lowers infectious dose
⭐ Conditions reducing gastric acid (achlorhydria, PPI use, gastrectomy) dramatically increase susceptibility to Salmonella, Vibrio, and Campylobacter
⭐ The elderly and infants are more susceptible because of diminished gastric acid production and immature immunity, respectively
Other host factors that increase susceptibility: immunodeficiency, inflammatory bowel disease, disruption of normal GI flora by broad-spectrum antibiotics

questions.stem: Which of the following bacterial agents has the lowest infective dose for producing gastrointestinal disease in the human host?
questions.explanation: The answer is D: Shigella flexneri. Both virulent E. coli varieties, V. cholerae, and nontyphoid Salmonella serotypes have an infective dose of around 10⁶ organisms. Nontyphoid Salmonella ID may be as high as 10⁹. Host factors that influence susceptibility include immunologic deficiencies, inflammatory bowel disease, disruption of GI flora from antibiotics, and use of acid-reducing agents. Shigella has the lowest infective dose among the choices — sometimes as low as 10 organisms — because it resists gastric acid and invades colonic epithelium very efficiently. Two other agents with similarly low infective doses (not among the choices) are Salmonella typhi and Campylobacter jejuni (~10²).
keypoints: ⭐ Shigella has one of the lowest infective doses of any enteric pathogen — as few as 10–200 organisms are sufficient to cause disease
⭐ Low infective dose explains why Shigellosis spreads easily via fecal-oral route in crowded settings (daycare, prisons, refugees)
⭐ In contrast, nontyphoid Salmonella requires 10⁶–10⁹ organisms; V. cholerae requires 10⁶–10⁸ (reduced by antacid use)
Campylobacter jejuni and S. typhi also have low infective doses (~10²), making them hypervirulent via the fecal-oral route

questions.stem: Intestinal infection with which of the following organisms should NOT be treated with antibiotics?
questions.explanation: The answer is B: Escherichia coli O157:H7. Infection with this strain of E. coli is associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). This complication may be more likely to occur if the patient is treated with antibiotics, because antibiotic-induced bacterial cell lysis releases large amounts of preformed Shiga toxin, dramatically increasing systemic toxin load. Cholera, typhoid fever, pseudomembranous colitis, and shigellosis all respond favorably to antibiotic treatment. Antimotility agents should also be avoided with EHEC for the same reason.
keypoints: ⭐ Antibiotics are CONTRAINDICATED in EHEC (E. coli O157:H7) infections — they increase Shiga toxin release and risk of HUS
⭐ HUS risk is highest in children <5 and elderly; supportive care (hydration, dialysis if needed) is the mainstay of treatment
⭐ All other enteric bacterial infections in the list (C. difficile, S. typhi, Shigella, V. cholerae) benefit from appropriate antibiotic therapy
Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide) in EHEC — they prolong mucosal exposure to toxin and increase HUS risk

questions.stem: A young man presents to the emergency department with a 1-day history of delirium. He has had a sustained fever of up to 40 °C and a history of progressive headache, myalgia, and constipation which began 10 days previously as he was returning to the United States from a trip to visit relatives in India. Physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and red spots on the chest and neck. Colonies of a Gram-negative bacillus that produced a characteristic "fish-eye" growth (lactose nonfermenter with sulfur reduction) are isolated on Hektoen agar from blood and stool samples as shown in the photograph. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The answer is E: Typhoid fever. The case is typical for typhoid fever caused by Salmonella typhi. This multiorgan system disease is due to dissemination of the microbe within macrophages. S. typhi enters the intestine, infects local macrophages, and is transported throughout the body, replicating in macrophages of the lymph nodes, spleen, liver, and bone marrow. The infection is accompanied by high fever and toxemia. Replication in Peyer's patches leads to bowel wall inflammation and subsequent constipation. Bacterial emboli to the skin cause the rose spots seen on the chest and neck. S. typhi is isolated on Hektoen agar, on which the production of hydrogen sulfide is demonstrated as a black center within the colony — the hallmark "fish-eye" appearance. Cholera causes watery diarrhea; HUS is caused by E. coli O157:H7 with bloody diarrhea and renal failure; Shigellosis causes bloody diarrhea; Tularemia can present as a typhoidal form but lacks these microbiological findings.
questions.imageAlt: Hektoen agar plate showing characteristic fish-eye colonies of Salmonella typhi with dark black centers (H₂S production) and translucent halos
questions.imageCaption: Hektoen agar: S. typhi 'fish-eye' colonies with black sulfur centers and pale halos — classic diagnostic appearance
keypoints: ⭐ Typhoid fever (S. typhi) presents with stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots, hepatosplenomegaly, and constipation early (vs. diarrhea later)
⭐ S. typhi on Hektoen agar produces characteristic 'fish-eye' colonies: black H₂S center with translucent halo (lactose nonfermenter + H₂S producer)
⭐ S. typhi disseminates intracellularly within macrophages to liver, spleen, bone marrow — causing a systemic illness, not just GI disease
Fluoroquinolones or third-generation cephalosporins are first-line treatment; chloramphenicol used historically

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male became ill with watery diarrhea due to a bacterial infection while on a trip to South America. Which of the following is the key event that promotes the development of watery diarrhea?
choices: Increase in the intestinal epithelial cell levels of cAMP
Increase in the levels of intracellular chloride
Movement of water from the intestinal lumen into the epithelial cells
Movement of ions such as potassium and sodium into the intestinal epithelial cells
questions.explanation: The answer is B: Increase in the intestinal epithelial cell levels of cAMP. Bacterial causes of watery diarrhea include Vibrio cholerae and enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC). Both produce toxins (cholera toxin and heat-labile toxin, respectively) whose active A subunit ADP-ribosylates the Gsα protein, permanently activating adenylate cyclase and causing a massive rise in intracellular cAMP. Elevated cAMP prevents sodium absorption into intestinal cells and massively increases chloride secretion out of cells. Water follows the chloride into the intestinal lumen by osmosis, producing the characteristic voluminous watery diarrhea.
keypoints: ⭐ Cholera toxin (and ETEC heat-labile toxin): ADP-ribosylates Gsα → constitutively active adenylate cyclase → ↑↑ cAMP → massive Cl⁻ secretion + Na⁺ absorption blocked → watery diarrhea
⭐ Key distinction: cAMP mechanism (cholera, ETEC) vs. cGMP mechanism (ETEC heat-stable toxin, STa)
⭐ Treatment is oral rehydration solution (ORS), not antibiotics — the fluid loss from rice-water stools can be several liters per hour
ETEC is the most common cause of traveler's diarrhea (watery, not bloody); cholera is endemic in South Asia/Africa

questions.stem: A 47-year-old male is diagnosed with peptic ulcer disease. Treatment includes antibiotics for infection of the stomach with Helicobacter pylori. Which enzyme is secreted by this organism and enables it to survive in the acid environment of the stomach?
questions.explanation: The answer is E: Urease. This enzyme neutralizes gastric acids by hydrolyzing urea to ammonia and CO₂. The ammonia raises the local pH, creating a more favorable microenvironment for H. pylori to survive. H. pylori also secretes catalase and superoxide dismutase, which provide resistance to killing by neutrophils, and mucinase, which breaks down gastric mucus, allowing the organism to contact gastric epithelial cells. Vacuolating cytotoxin (VacA) is another important virulence factor that leads to epithelial cell injury and neutrophil infiltration.
keypoints: ⭐ Urease is the primary survival mechanism of H. pylori: urea → NH₃ (raises local pH) + CO₂
⭐ Urease is also the basis of the urea breath test and urease rapid test (CLO test) used for diagnosis
⭐ H. pylori also produces catalase, superoxide dismutase (resist neutrophil killing), mucinase (mucus penetration), and VacA (epithelial injury)
H. pylori is a microaerophilic, Gram-negative curved rod with polar flagella; it colonizes the gastric antrum preferentially

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with diarrhea, malaise, fever, and abdominal pain. The stools were positive for occult blood and fecal leukocytes. Microscopy of the stool also reveals the presence of curved bacilli that moved about on a slide in a darting motion. The etiologic agent, a Gram-negative, curved rod, grew on specialized medium in microaerophilic conditions. Which one of the following organisms is most likely responsible for the disease?
questions.explanation: The answer is A: Campylobacter jejuni. All organisms listed cause diarrhea; however, only C. jejuni and Salmonella sp. typically cause bloody diarrhea. Shigella flexneri causes bloody diarrhea whereas S. sonnei typically causes watery diarrhea. Of the organisms listed, only C. jejuni is a microaerophilic (requiring reduced oxygen), Gram-negative, curved rod that demonstrates characteristic darting motility when viewed under a microscope. C. jejuni grows on Skirrow or Campy-CVA selective agar at 42°C under microaerophilic conditions (5% O₂, 10% CO₂).
keypoints: ⭐ Campylobacter jejuni: Gram-negative curved/spiral rod, darting corkscrew motility, microaerophilic growth at 42°C
⭐ Most common cause of bacterial gastroenteritis in the United States; associated with undercooked poultry and unpasteurized milk
⭐ Bloody diarrhea + fecal leukocytes = inflammatory diarrhea; Campylobacter and Salmonella are the top two causes
Post-infectious complication: Guillain-Barré syndrome (molecular mimicry between C. jejuni LPS and gangliosides GM1/GD1b)

questions.stem: Five adults and seven children in a village in South Africa present over several days to a local clinic with voluminous watery diarrhea containing flecks of mucus. They show signs of severe dehydration and are treated with oral fluids and electrolytes. Stool cultures grew yellow colonies on thiosulfate citrate bile salt (TCBS) media. What is the etiology of this outbreak?
questions.explanation: The answer is D: Vibrio cholerae. The case describes an outbreak of cholera characterized by abundant 'rice-water' stools and rapid severe dehydration. The organism grows as yellow colonies on TCBS (thiosulfate citrate bile salt sucrose) agar because V. cholerae ferments sucrose, turning the indicator dye yellow. Non-01/non-0139 Vibrio species grow as blue-green colonies on TCBS (non-sucrose fermenters). The other organisms listed typically cause bloody diarrhea or have different microbiologic characteristics.
keypoints: ⭐ V. cholerae on TCBS agar: yellow colonies (sucrose fermenter) — key lab identifier
⭐ Cholera toxin: ADP-ribosylates Gsα → ↑ cAMP → Cl⁻ secretion → rice-water stools (up to 20 L/day), rapid dehydration
⭐ Treatment: aggressive oral/IV rehydration is primary; antibiotics (doxycycline/azithromycin) shorten duration
V. cholerae O1 (El Tor biotype) and O139 cause epidemic cholera; endemic in South Asia and parts of Africa

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with fever, nausea, severe abdominal cramping, and bloody diarrhea that was fecal leukocyte-positive. A few days previously, she had eaten undercooked chicken. Of the following, which is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: The answer is A: Campylobacter jejuni. This organism and nontyphoid strains of Salmonella are associated with ingestion of undercooked chicken or raw eggs. Both are common causes of foodborne infections in the United States and both cause a bloody diarrhea that is fecal leukocyte-positive. C. perfringens food poisoning is associated with contaminated meat products but causes an intoxication characterized by abdominal cramps and watery (not bloody) diarrhea occurring 8 to 24 hours after ingestion. S. typhi and S. dysenteriae are strict human pathogens and are not associated with undercooked chicken. Y. enterocolitica infection is generally associated with contaminated dairy products and is uncommon in the United States.
keypoints: ⭐ Campylobacter jejuni is the leading cause of foodborne bacterial diarrhea in the US; the #1 source is undercooked chicken
⭐ Key features: bloody diarrhea, fecal leukocytes (invasive), fever, crampy abdominal pain — mimics inflammatory bowel disease
⭐ C. perfringens causes watery (not bloody) diarrhea 8–24 h after ingestion of reheated meats — no fecal leukocytes (toxin-mediated)
Campylobacter gastroenteritis is usually self-limited; azithromycin or fluoroquinolones are used for severe/prolonged cases

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy developed bloody diarrhea after eating a poorly cooked hamburger. A few days later, he was hospitalized with oliguria and hypertension. With which organism is he most likely infected?
questions.explanation: The answer is D: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli. The case is descriptive of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) associated with infection with E. coli O157:H7. This strain produces phage-associated Shiga toxins (Stx-1 and/or Stx-2) that are functionally and antigenically similar to those produced by Shigella dysenteriae. The toxins damage renal endothelial cells, causing the hallmark triad of HUS: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure (manifested here as oliguria). Undercooked ground beef is the classic vehicle. C. perfringens causes watery diarrhea from a preformed toxin. S. typhi is rare in the US and causes typhoid fever, not HUS. Enteroinvasive E. coli causes Shigella-like dysentery without HUS. Y. enterocolitica causes a milder diarrheal illness.
keypoints: ⭐ Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC/EHEC O157:H7): undercooked hamburger → bloody diarrhea → HUS in children
⭐ HUS = microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute renal failure (oliguria, ↑ creatinine)
⭐ Shiga toxin binds Gb3 receptors on renal endothelial cells → endothelial injury → thrombotic microangiopathy
Antibiotics are contraindicated — they increase Shiga toxin release and worsen HUS prognosis

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to an urgent care facility with severe vomiting. She claims that several other people who ate at the church picnic 4 hours earlier are also sick with the same symptoms. She is clinically diagnosed with food poisoning. A health department investigation reveals that all affected individuals had eaten the ham salad. What is the bacterial agent responsible for the signs and symptoms?
questions.explanation: The answer is E: Staphylococcus aureus. This organism, a frequent skin colonizer, can contaminate food during preparation. Food is then left at room temperature for several hours, during which bacteria replicate and secrete heat-stable enterotoxins. The toxins enter the blood and affect the vomiting control center of the brain, inducing vomiting 1 to 6 hours following ingestion. The incubation period of 4 hours, predominantly vomiting (not diarrhea), and the association with a salty cured meat (ham salad) are classic for S. aureus food poisoning. Foods most frequently implicated include salted meats, ham, potato or macaroni salad, and cream-filled pastries. C. jejuni causes diarrheal illness associated with undercooked chicken. C. perfringens causes watery diarrhea (8–24 h) from reheated meats. B. cereus emetic form is associated with fried rice (1–6 h). Salmonella food poisoning causes bloody diarrhea 16 h to 2 days after ingestion.
keypoints: ⭐ S. aureus food poisoning: 1–6 hour incubation (preformed heat-stable toxin), predominantly VOMITING, no fever
⭐ The heat-stable enterotoxin acts as a superantigen on vagal nerve endings → emesis center stimulation
⭐ Classic foods: ham, potato/macaroni salad, cream-filled pastries — high-salt or high-sugar foods handled by colonized food workers
Compare: C. perfringens (8–24 h, watery diarrhea, reheated meat), B. cereus emetic (1–6 h, fried rice), Salmonella (16 h–2 days, bloody diarrhea)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with fever, abdominal pain, and tenderness in the right lower quadrant. A white blood cell count reveals leukocytosis. Suspecting appendicitis, the child is taken to surgery; however, the removed appendix is grossly and histologically normal. The bacterial cause for the boy's symptoms was subsequently identified as a Gram-negative rod after cold enrichment of fecal cultures. What is the etiology of this infection?
questions.explanation: The answer is E: Yersinia enterocolitica. This Gram-negative rod usually causes a diarrheal illness but can also cause infections that mimic appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis) due to mesenteric lymphadenitis and terminal ileitis. Y. enterocolitica is part of the normal intestinal flora of cattle and other farm animals. Human infection occurs by ingestion of food or water contaminated with animal feces. The organism is able to grow at refrigerated temperatures (4°C) while other organisms present in the same fecal sample cannot — this isolation technique is known as cold enrichment. S. typhi and C. jejuni have been isolated from diseased appendices but are isolated at 37°C. C. difficile is an anaerobic Gram-positive rod. Vibrio parahaemolyticus causes a diarrheal illness following ingestion of raw seafood.
keypoints: ⭐ Yersinia enterocolitica causes pseudoappendicitis: right lower quadrant pain mimicking appendicitis (mesenteric lymphadenitis + terminal ileitis)
⭐ Cold enrichment (4°C growth) is the diagnostic clue — Y. enterocolitica is psychrotrophic; it thrives at refrigerator temperature
⭐ Source: pork products, contaminated water, farm animals (especially swine); transmitted fecal-orally
Other Yersinia: Y. pestis (plague, non-motile at 37°C), Y. pseudotuberculosis (also pseudoappendicitis, less common)
